name: Abiram
title: Reubenite who rebelled against Moses
summary: Abiram, son of Eliab from the tribe of Reuben, was a central figure in the great rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron during the wilderness journey. Together with his brother Dathan, he joined the Levite Korah's revolt, where On ben Pelet is also mentioned at the outset. While Korah challenged the exclusivity of the Aaronic priesthood, Dathan and Abiram directed their opposition against Moses' political authority. They accused Moses of leading the people away from Egypt's abundance only to rule over them in the wilderness, and they refused to obey his summons. As divine judgment, the earth opened up and swallowed Abiram, Dathan, and their families alive. This dramatic event became a powerful warning example in Israel's collective memory about the seriousness of rebelling against the order God has established.

keyEvents.title: The Rebellion Against Moses and Aaron
keyEvents.description: Abiram joined with Korah, Dathan, and On son of Pelet in rebelling against the leadership of Moses and Aaron. They challenged the existing order, claiming that the entire congregation was holy and that Moses and Aaron had exalted themselves above the Lord's assembly.

keyEvents.title: Refused to Meet Moses
keyEvents.description: When Moses sent for Dathan and Abiram, they refused to come. They accused Moses of having brought them out of a land flowing with milk and honey—ironically meaning Egypt—only to let them die in the wilderness, and charged him with seeking to rule over them.

keyEvents.title: Stood defiantly by their tents
keyEvents.description: Abiram and Datan stood defiantly at the entrance to their tents together with their wives, sons, and little children when the final judgment was about to fall.

keyEvents.title: The earth opened up
keyEvents.description: God judged the rebels by opening the earth and swallowing Abiram, Datan, and their families along with everything they owned. They went down alive into Sheol, and the earth closed over them.

keyEvents.title: A warning example
keyEvents.description: Abiram's fate was remembered as a serious warning against rebellion against God's appointed leaders. The event is mentioned later in the books of Moses and in the Psalms as an example of God's righteous judgment on those who challenge His order.

versions.summary: Abiram was a Reubenite who, together with Datan, Korah, and On, led a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. He and his co-conspirators were swallowed by the earth as God's judgment on their rebellion, which became a warning example for the people of Israel.
versions.title: The rebel against Moses
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'leader' is somewhat imprecise. Abiram was not a leader in the formal sense, but rather a rebel leader/rebel. It should be clarified that he was a tribal chief or head of the tribe of Reuben who led a rebellion.; [major] According to Numbers 26:9, Abiram's brothers were Dathan and Nemuel. However, Nemuel is mentioned in Numbers 26:9 as a son of Eliab together with Dathan and Abiram. Yet in Genesis 26:9 and Numbers 16:1, no Nemuel is mentioned as a brother. In Numbers 26:9, Dathan and Abiram are named as sons of Eliab, but Nemuel is another person – either a son of Simeon (Numbers 26:12) or a son of Eliab (as some read Numbers 26:9). The data should be carefully verified. Traditionally, Dathan is regarded as Abiram's brother (both sons of Eliab), while Nemuel as a brother is more uncertain.; [minor] The summary is good but could advantageously mention that Korah's rebellion primarily concerned the priesthood, whereas Dathan and Abiram's rebellion was directed against Moses' civil leadership. This nuance makes the profile more precise.; [minor] The title 'The Rebel Against Moses' is appropriate but could include his tribal background for more context, e.g., 'A Reubenite Who Revolted Against Moses'.; [minor] In the final event ('A Warning Example'), reference is made to Psalm 106:17. BookId 19 is the book of Psalms, and chapter 106 is correct. The reference is accurate.; [major] The profile lacks footnotes. There are interesting historical, linguistic, and theological details that should be included, such as the meaning of the name Abiram, the theological significance of the earth opening up, and Korah's rebellion in Jewish tradition.

versions.summary: Abiram was the son of Eliab from the tribe of Reuben. Together with his brother Dathan, the Levite Korah and On, he led a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. While Korah and his Levites challenged Aaron's priesthood, Dathan and Abiram's revolt was directed at Moses' civil authority. They accused Moses of bringing the people out of Egypt only to rule over them. As God's judgment on the rebellion, the earth opened up and swallowed Abiram, Dathan and their families. The event became a warning example in Israel's history about the consequences of rebelling against God's chosen leaders.
versions.title: Reubenite who rebelled against Moses
versions.reason: [minor] Abiram is not described as a 'tribal leader' in the Bible. He was a prominent man in the tribe of Reuben, but there is no basis for calling him a tribal leader. A more accurate role would be 'prominent Reubenite' or similar.; [minor] The phrasing 'While Korah and his Levites challenged Aaron's priesthood, Datan and Abiram's rebellion was directed against Moses' civil authority' is a good theological distinction, but it should be clarified that On (son of Pelet) is mentioned in Num 16:1 but then disappears from the narrative. Saying he 'led' the rebellion may be an overinterpretation.; [minor] The claim that 'the whole congregation was holy' is primarily Korah's argument (Num 16:3), not necessarily Abiram's specific complaint. Abiram's complaints (vv. 12–14) are more directed at Moses' political leadership. It may be useful to differentiate this more clearly.

footnotes.text: The name Abiram (אֲבִירָם) is composed of אָב (av, 'father') and רָם (ram, 'exalted'). The meaning is 'my father is exalted' or 'the father of the Exalted One'. The name's connotation of exaltation stands in sharp contrast to Abiram's fate – he who sought exaltation was literally lowered into the earth.

Korah's rebellion (Num 16) was a complex uprising with at least two distinct factions: Korah and his 250 Levites challenged the exclusivity of the Aaronic priesthood, while Datan and Abiram from the tribe of Reuben challenged Moses' civil and political leadership. The involvement of the Reubenites may be connected to the fact that Reuben was Jacob's firstborn son, and the tribe may have felt their natural right to leadership was bypassed by Moses and Aaron from the tribe of Levi.

In rabbinic tradition (Mishnah, Sanhedrin 10:3), Datan and Abiram are counted among those who have no share in the world to come. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 109b) elaborates that they were notorious troublemakers already in Egypt and identifies them with the two Hebrews who quarreled in Exod 2:13. On ben Pelet is mentioned in Num 16:1 but then disappears from the narrative – according to rabbinic tradition, he was saved because his wife persuaded him to withdraw from the rebellion.

The opening of the earth and swallowing of the rebels is a unique act of judgment in the biblical narrative. This dramatic form of judgment – where they went down alive into Sheol (שְׁאוֹל, sheol) – emphasized that it was God Himself, not Moses, who judged. The event became a paradigmatic example of divine judgment in later biblical literature, referenced in Deut 11:6 and Ps 106:17.

The area around Kadesh-Barnea in the northern Negev, where the rebellion is traditionally placed, has geological formations with cracks and unstable ground. The region is characterized by limestone and chalk formations that can form sinkholes. Although this does not prove the biblical account, it provides a natural geological context for the event described.
